## Today's Agenda

- A report that rebuilds itself
- IMRaD, and the three transparency markers
- Two studio blocks: the paper, then the poster
- Publishing, and the checks that run first

## The Last Meeting

[Studio session]{.eyebrow}

- **Two working blocks:** the White Paper, then the poster
    - Short input from me between them, the rest is yours
    - I am circulating all evening
- **What we build today is what you submit**
- **Leave with a rendered site, a layout, and a reflection**

## Done, and Not Finished

- **The study has every hard part behind it**
    - A question, a theory, a reliability-tested codebook
    - A defensible sample, a clean dataset, three figures, a finding
- **And it lives in pieces**
    - A codebook here, a script there, output that scrolled past

A study scattered across a dozen files is raw material. Today gives it a form.

## A Report That Rebuilds Itself

- **The ordinary way is quietly fragile**
    - Run, copy numbers, screenshot figures, write around them
    - Change one rule and every pasted number is stale
    - Nothing in the document says so
- **The alternative: put the analysis inside the document**
    - A **Quarto document** interleaves prose with live code chunks

## Numbers You Never Type

```markdown
The analysis dataset held `r nrow(analysis)` coded messages,
of which `r sum(!is.na(analysis$is_gaming))` carried a
gaming-status label.
```

In the rendered report those backtick expressions become the actual counts, so nothing in
the sentence can fall out of date.

## Figures You Never Paste

```r
#| label: fig-msglen
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Message length by channel type."

ggplot(msglen, aes(message_length, fill = is_gaming)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5) +
  v2v::theme_v2v()
```

Those lines sit inside an `{r}` chunk in the report, so the figure is produced at render
time rather than pasted in.

## Two Payoffs That Matter

- **The report cannot drift**, because it is the analysis
- **The report can be checked**
    - Anyone with the source and data renders the same results (Peng, 2011)
- **The idea predates Quarto and R**
    - Runnable code and its prose in one document
    - Knuth named it **literate programming** in 1984

The "one click" is the render button.

## IMRaD, and What Each Section Owes

- **Introduction:** the question and why it matters, your prospectus
- **Methods:** what was done, in enough detail to repeat
    - Codebook, sampling, reliability, wrangling
- **Results:** what was found, without interpretation
    - Figures, means, the statistic with df, p, and effect size
- **Discussion:** what it means, plus the honest limits

An abstract in front, references at the back.

## The White Paper, Specifically

- **IMRaD structure, APA 7th edition throughout**
- **Effect sizes and power statistics**, not only p-values
- **A pre-registration disclosure** in the Methods
- **A Discussion that situates the finding** in your literature

Converting results into IMRaD costs something. Ask what is lost, and what must be added.

## Methods, Three Transparency Markers

1. A **data provenance** statement: where the data came from, and how
2. An **intercoder reliability** report: coefficient, protocol, threshold
3. The **pre-registration disclosure**, with its OSF URL

Each signals that the study meets the standard it claims. Anything beyond the plan is
labeled **exploratory**.

## What Preregistration Is For

> "Preregistration distinguishes analyses and outcomes that result from predictions from
> those that result from postdictions."
>
> Nosek et al. (2018, p. 2600)

- **Not a promise of virtue**, but a way of making a distinction legible
- **Draft your disclosure sentence today**
    - List your deviations, and say how you report each

## Where the 200 Points Sit

- **Introduction and framing:** 25
- **Methods:** 55
- **Results:** 40
- **Discussion:** 40
- **Abstract and references:** 15
- **Reproducibility and publication:** 15
- **Reflection:** 10

Methods carries the most weight because it carries the transparency markers.

## Not Only a Threshold {.discuss}

[Wasserstein and Lazar (2016)]{.eyebrow}

> "Scientific conclusions and business or policy decisions should not be based only on
> whether a p-value passes a specific threshold."
>
> Wasserstein and Lazar (2016, p. 131)

- The word doing the work is *only*
- What else does your White Paper put beside it?
- A reader who ignores your p: what convinces them?

## One Site, Many Pages

```yaml
project:
  type: website

website:
  title: "Twitch Chat Study"
  navbar:
    left:
      - text: "Report"
        href: index.qmd
      - text: "Codebook"
        href: codebook.qmd
```

`_quarto.yml` names the site and lists its pages, turning a folder of `.qmd` files into
one navigable site.

## Studio Block One

[White Paper]{.eyebrow}

- **Get `index.qmd` rendering**, even if it is mostly headings
- **Move your Results in first**, since you already have it
- **Replace every pasted number** with an inline `r` expression
- **Replace every pasted figure** with a chunk that produces it
- **Then write the Discussion paragraph** reporting size and significance

## Going Live

```r
v2v::deploy_portfolio()
```

```
Pre-flight checks
  renv library in sync ......... ok
  no uncommitted changes ....... ok
  _quarto.yml valid ............ ok

Rendering 4 pages ... done
Live at: https://username.github.io/twitch-chat-study/
```

## The Three Pre-Flight Checks

- **renv in sync:** built with the versions the source declares
- **No uncommitted changes:** live matches what is saved
- **`_quarto.yml` valid:** the render will not fail partway
- **Each heads off a demoralizing failure**
    - The last being a collapse the night a portfolio is due

The checks exist so the last step of a long study is the calm one.

## The Poster

- **36 by 24 inches**, landscape orientation
- **Title, authors, institution**, and a 100-word abstract
- **Background and hypotheses**, then condensed methods
- **Key results** with one or two `theme_v2v()` figures
- **Discussion and implications**, plus a **QR code**

## What Earns Space on a Poster

- **A ninety-second pitch**, not a paper at a larger font
- **Pick the one figure that lands the finding in thirty seconds**
    - Give it the most space on the board
- **Cut every sentence that shows effort rather than result**
- **Numbers survive, hedges do not**

Your reader is standing up, holding a drink, four feet away.

## Studio Block Two

[Poster]{.eyebrow}

- **Sketch the layout on paper first**, in blocks, before software
- **Place your chosen figure**, then build the text around it
- **Write the 100-word abstract last**, once the blocks exist
- **Generate the QR code** from the URL the deploy gave you
- **Read your title aloud**, and cut it if it takes two breaths

## Common Failures in the Last Week

- **Rendering on your machine and nowhere else**, because renv drifted
- **A figure that vanishes in the site**
    - Its chunk depends on an object made in your console
- **A poster exported at screen resolution**, printed at 36 inches
- **A QR code pointing at a private repository**

Test the whole chain today, on a machine you did not build it on.

## The Reflection

- **One paragraph, and the portfolio is incomplete without it**
    - What turned out harder than expected
    - Where a coding rule proved ambiguous in practice
    - What the dataset could not answer, and why
- **Resist the bland version and the anxious one**

A reflection is evidence of judgment, not an apology.

## Checkpoint Before You Leave

You should have:

- A portfolio site that renders locally with no errors
- A Results section with zero hand-typed numbers
- A published URL, and a QR code pointing at it
- A poster layout with its main figure chosen and placed
- The reflection paragraph drafted, even roughly

## From Vibes to Variables

- **A question became a design, and a design became data**
- **Data became figures and a test**
- **All of it became a site another person can check and extend**
- **The dataset happened to be Twitch chat**, and nothing depended on that

The distance from vibes to variables is the whole of research methods, and you have now
walked it once.
